tasks.q: What must hold before binary search is used?
a: The data is sorted by the search key
tasks.fb: The data is sorted by the search key

tasks.q: Binary search on unsorted data can...
a: Discard the half containing the target
tasks.fb: Discard the half containing the target. The list must be ordered.

tasks.q: Match each comparison to the update.
tasks.fb: Remove the checked midpoint as well as the impossible half.

tasks.q: If target < data[mid], which update is correct?
tasks.fb: high = mid - 1. If target is greater, move low above mid.

tasks.q: Search this list for 21. Checked values?

tasks.fb: 5. Recalculate the midpoint after each update.

tasks.q: For target 1 in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], what is checked?
When low > high, the remaining range is...
tasks.fb: Empty. A search can exhaust the remaining range.

tasks.q: Which is the strongest case for binary search?
a: Many lookups in a large sorted list
One lookup in three unsorted items
A list that cannot be ordered
A target known to be the first item
tasks.fb: Many lookups in a large sorted list

tasks.q: Why can binary search scale well?
a: It discards about half the remaining items each time
It checks all items every time
tasks.fb: It discards about half the remaining items each time. Binary search can use fewer comparisons.

tasks.q: Order the checks for target 14 in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14].
What is the worst-case advantage as a sorted list grows?
a: Binary search repeatedly halves the remaining range
Binary search checks every item twice
Linear search always checks fewer items
tasks.fb: Binary search repeatedly halves the remaining range

info.title: Sorted data first
info.text:
The list must be ordered.

Use the order to rule out one half.

Unsorted data makes this reasoning unsafe.

Challenge: Why is sorted order required?

It guarantees smaller values lie before the middle and larger values after it.

info.title: Find the midpoint
info.text:
Use low and high indices.

Take the integer midpoint.

Our examples round down.

Challenge: What is mid when low = 3 and high = 8?

(3 + 8) DIV 2 = 5.

info.title: Discard the wrong half
info.text:
If target is greater, move low above mid.

If target is smaller, move high below mid.

The middle item has already been checked.

Challenge: Why use mid + 1 rather than mid?

The midpoint has already failed to match and should not remain in the search range.

info.title: Trace a successful search
info.text:
Recalculate the midpoint after each update.

Count comparisons with the target.

Stop immediately at a match.

Challenge: What values are checked when searching for 6?

12, then 6. The target is found after two comparisons.

info.title: Trace not found
info.text:
A search can exhaust the remaining range.

Stop when low is greater than high.

Do not access another midpoint after stopping.

Challenge: Why does low > high mean not found?

No indices remain in the possible search range.

info.title: Choose the search
info.text:
Binary search can use fewer comparisons.

Sorting first also takes work.

Consider list size and repeated searches.

Challenge: Why not always sort before a one-off search?

Sorting takes work. For a short unsorted list, one linear scan may be simpler and cheaper overall.
